readerTitle: The two-minute answer that costs you 50 hours a year
caseNote: 가상 사례 (신발 매장, 물류 창고) + 실제 연구 (생성 효과, Slamecka & Graf 1978) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 코칭은 시간이 드는 친절이 아니라, 처음에 시간을 더 쓰고 나중에 반복되는 질문을 없애는 투자다.
misconception: 답을 바로 알려주는 것이 가장 빠르고 효율적이다. 코칭은 시간 여유가 있을 때나 하는 것이다.

sources.text: Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4(6), 592–604.
매장·창고 사례와 모든 시간 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 훅 계산: 하루 6번 × 2분 × 주 5일 × 52주 = 3,120분 = 52시간. 카드에는 "more than 50 hours"로 적었습니다.
생성 효과(generation effect)는 스스로 만들어 낸 정보를 읽은 정보보다 더 잘 기억하는 경향입니다. 원 연구는 단어 기억 실험이므로 카드에서는 "tend to remember"로 일반화 수준만 적었습니다. 직장 코칭 효과를 직접 입증한 연구로 쓰지 않았는지 확인하세요.
네 가지 질문 순서는 GROW 모델과 비슷하지만 상표·프레임워크 이름을 쓰지 않고 원리만 소개했습니다.

cards.title: The two-minute answer that costs you 50 hours a year
body: Maya runs a busy shoe store. About six times a day, her shift lead Sam walks over: "A customer wants this. What should I do?"
Maya answers in two minutes. It feels efficient. Over a year, those quick answers add up to more than 50 hours. And Sam still asks.

image.label: A store manager answering the same question again and again
image.brief: 신발 매장 계산대 옆. 매니저가 직원의 질문에 답하는 같은 장면이 여러 겹으로 반복되어 겹쳐 보이고, 벽시계 바늘이 빠르게 돌아가는 모션 라인. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sam needs an answer.
body: Sam asks: a customer wants to return worn shoes without a receipt. What should he do?
You know the answer. You have five minutes before a delivery arrives.

options.text: Tell him: offer store credit, not a cash refund
options.feedback: Fast and correct, and this customer is handled. But Sam learns the answer, not the thinking, so he'll be back with the next odd return.

options.text: Ask: "What do you think we should do, and why?" Then add what he missed
options.feedback: It costs a few extra minutes now. In return, Sam practices the judgment he'll need when you aren't there.

options.text: Tell him to read the returns policy and figure it out
options.feedback: It saves your time, but Sam may guess wrong in front of the customer. He also learns that asking you is unwelcome.

cards.title: Slower at first. Then much faster.
body: Assume coaching takes 8 minutes instead of 2. After two weeks, Sam handles four of every six questions on his own.
Coaching is behind until about **week 11**. After that, it wins every single week.

breakdown.label: Telling, every week
breakdown.detail: 6 questions × 2 min × 5 days. It never drops.

breakdown.label: Saved in year one
breakdown.detail: 52 hours of telling vs about 25 with coaching

cards.title: Coaching
body: **Coaching** means helping someone get better at solving problems by asking questions that make them think, instead of handing them the answer.
It is different from feedback, which tells people how past work landed, and from delegating, which hands over a task. Coaching builds the judgment that makes delegating safe.
cards.softwareNote: A senior engineer who answers every "how should I build this?" in chat becomes the team's bottleneck. Asking "What options did you consider?" takes longer this week and frees their calendar later.

cards.title: Four questions, in order.
body: A simple coaching conversation moves through four questions:
list: **What do you want to happen?** Agree on the goal
**What could you do?** Ask for at least two options
**What will you do?** Let them choose, then add what they missed
cards.callout: Why it sticks: psychologists call it the *generation effect*. People tend to remember answers they produce themselves better than answers they are handed.

cards.title: Telling moves an answer. Coaching moves a way of thinking.
body: The time math undersells coaching. Three months later, a customer asks Sam about something Maya never covered.
Sam walks through the same four questions in his head and handles it. When Maya takes a week off, the store keeps running instead of waiting for her phone to ring.

cards.title: Sometimes you should just tell.
list: **Emergencies and safety:** give a clear instruction now. Talk it through later
**Complete beginners:** they can't find answers they've never seen. Teach the basics first
**Decisions you've already made:** steering someone to your answer with questions feels like a quiz. Say what you want
cards.callout: Coaching pays back on problems that repeat. Spend the extra minutes there.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You supervise a distribution warehouse. Three people come to you in the same hour. Which one deserves a coaching conversation?

options.text: A new hire, on day one, asks how the handheld scanner works
options.feedback: Worth your time, but this is teaching, not coaching. They have nothing to reason from yet, so show them.

options.text: An experienced packer asks how to cut breakage on fragile orders
options.feedback: It's a recurring problem, and they know the work better than anyone. Their own fix is likely to be good and to stick.

options.text: A forklift driver asks if a pallet over the rated weight is fine to lift
options.feedback: Asking "what do you think?" here wastes seconds on a safety risk. Say no clearly, then talk it through afterward.

cards.title: Answer once, and you'll answer again tomorrow. Coach once, and the question starts to disappear.
body: Coaching costs more today and less every week after.
**Try it today:** the next time someone brings you a question you've answered before, ask first: "What do you think we should do?"
